A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same energy GNN research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable matching across the revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-task experiments and asynchronous-inference simulations in Tables 1–2, plus author-run benchmark experiments in Appendix G alongside cited results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds peptide-task results and asynchronous benchmark evaluations in Appendix G, Tables 5–6.

M1.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B–C retain the PICNN energy objective, local gradient messages, node-wise and edge-wise variants, attention mechanism, and implicit differentiation. Newly disclosed solver settings do not establish a change to the proposed method.

E1.justification: v2 retains the five synthetic tasks and MUTAG, PROTEINS, and PPI, while adding Peptides-func multilabel graph classification and Peptides-struct graph regression on 15,535 peptide graphs. Appendix G also extends asynchronous evaluation to the real-world benchmarks, substantially broadening task and test-scenario coverage.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds published GIN results from Xu et al. (2019) to the MUTAG and PROTEINS comparisons. The other existing comparator memberships are retained. Table 2's implicit-model comparisons remain summarized in its caption despite removal of their displayed rows.

E3.justification: Appendix E changes the reported asynchrony bound from B=7, defined as S+D, to B=5. This is a reported setting revision; identical retained Table 2 scores do not establish that experiments were rerun. Added peptide evaluations use the cited benchmark splits and AP/MAE metrics, while new asynchronous benchmark tests use ten test samples and one trained model instance.

E4.justification: v1 evaluates asynchronous degradation on synthetic tasks in Table 2. v2 adds corresponding robustness tests on MUTAG, PROTEINS, PPI, Peptides-func, and Peptides-struct in Table 6, extending evidence for the paper's central robustness claim to real-world benchmarks. The existing synthetic checks and architectural-variant comparisons remain.

E5.justification: Existing seed, fold, and mean/standard-deviation reporting is retained. Table 6 extends the established convention of reporting means and standard deviations across five asynchronous runs. No new uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test, or increased repeated-run count is reported.

E6.justification: Tables 5–6 add peptide performance and asynchronous benchmark results. For example, the attention energy GNN achieves 0.381 AP on Peptides-func, while GAT achieves the lowest Peptides-struct MAE, 0.335. Table 3 adds GIN scores, and Table 4 changes the quoted GraphSAGE score from 78.6 to 76.8 with revised attribution. Existing author-run synchronous scores are unchanged; these additions do not demonstrate same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 revises the formal timestamp definition: v1 requires tau_i^j(t) to belong to node j's update times, whereas v2 removes that restriction and allows current-time views under instantaneous communication. The convergence propositions and Appendix D proof otherwise retain their substance. The smoothness conditions made explicit in Proposition 4.2 were already assumed in v1 Section 3.2.

C1.justification: v2 drops the explicit 'first unified framework' novelty claim and focuses the abstract and introduction on state representations for decentralized agents. The principal claims about conditional asynchronous robustness and the novel energy GNN remain. Benchmark competitiveness is still claimed in the introduction despite its omission from the revised abstract.

C2.justification: Section 8 adds a conditional warm-start argument for slowly changing graphs and expands conditioning and numerical-instability limitations. Appendix G distinguishes matched-capacity comparisons from larger published models and leaves larger energy GNNs to future work. v1's explicit caveat that partial-asynchrony assumptions may not match real-world systems is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix F.2 newly specifies IGNN's convergence tolerance of 1e-5 and 500-iteration cap, and L-BFGS with tolerance 1e-5 and a 50-iteration cap for optimization-based GNNs. Appendix E discloses S=5 and D=2, while Tables 3–4 add cited-model dimensions and clearer provenance. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified implementations.

R1.justification: Section 7 replaces the historical asynchronous-algorithm and distributed-training survey with direct discussion of Dudzik et al. (2023), Monteagudo-Lago et al. (2024), and Faber and Wattenhofer (2024). It distinguishes their execution models from this work, replacing v1's assertion that no asynchronous GNN inference work was known. Multi-agent literature is moved into and expanded within the introduction.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around agent state representations, the contribution bullets become prose, the preliminaries are streamlined, and the related-work and conclusion discussions are substantially revised. The overall section and appendix sequence remains recognizable, but the narrative changes exceed local copyediting.

P2.justification: v2 adopts conference formatting and substantially restructures Tables 3–4, separating author-run and literature results and adding model-size and source labels. It adds Tables 5–6 and condenses Table 2's implicit-model rows into its caption. Figure 1's graphic is unchanged, although its caption is revised.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies missing solver settings, clarifies capacity differences behind benchmark comparisons, and addresses closely related asynchronous GNN research omitted from v1. These changes improve reproducibility and interpretation, while the new peptide and asynchronous benchmark results provide useful additional support. The added robustness estimates remain limited to one trained model and ten test samples, so the evidence supports a limited overall quality gain.
